nameStory: The Woodland Giant Wolf Spider gets its name from being one of the largest wolf spiders found in forested areas of the eastern United States. Like all wolf spiders, it's named for its hunting style - these arachnids don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively hunt and chase down their meals like wolves pursuing their quarry. The 'giant' part certainly fits, as this impressive spider can reach up to an inch in body length!
description: The Woodland Giant Wolf Spider is a robust, hunting spider that can grow impressively large - up to one inch in body length, not counting the legs. This makes it one of the biggest spiders you're likely to encounter in New England's forests. Unlike web-building spiders, this is an active hunter with a sturdy, athletic build designed for chasing down prey. Its overall appearance is typically brown and gray with mottled patterns that help it blend into the forest floor.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body reaches up to one inch long - about the size of a quarter without the legs. When you include the legs, it can span nearly three inches across, making it noticeably larger than most other spiders you'll find.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Robust and athletic-looking with a distinctly chunky, powerful build. The body feels solid and substantial compared to the more delicate appearance of web-building spiders.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in three rows - two large eyes in front, two medium ones behind those, and four smaller eyes in the back row. The front-facing eyes give it an alert, almost intelligent expression.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray coloration with darker patterns that create excellent camouflage against bark, leaves, and forest debris. The patterns often have a subtle tiger-stripe quality.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Runs quickly across the ground when disturbed, often stopping suddenly and remaining motionless when it thinks it's hidden. No web - this spider actively hunts its prey.

habitat: Look for Woodland Giant Wolf Spiders in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with plenty of leaf litter and fallen logs. They prefer well-drained woodland floors where they can hunt among the decomposing leaves and organic debris. You might spot them near hiking trails, in camping areas, or around the edges of forest clearings where they hunt for insects and other small prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active hunters. This is when you're most likely to see them moving around during warmer days as they search for mates and food after the long winter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered. Females may be seen carrying round egg sacs attached to their spinnerets, looking like they're carrying a small pearl.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek shelter for winter. Spiderlings that hatched earlier in the year are growing larger and more noticeable.
seasonality.winter: Adults hide under logs, rocks, and deep leaf litter, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns. Very rarely seen during cold months.

funFact: Mother Woodland Giant Wolf Spiders are incredibly devoted parents - after their eggs hatch, dozens of tiny spiderlings climb onto mom's back and ride around for up to a week, creating what looks like a living, moving carpet of baby spiders that will scatter in all directions if disturbed!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large, brown spiders like fishing spiders or grass spiders. Remember that wolf spiders are ground hunters with no web, while fishing spiders are usually near water and grass spiders build funnel-shaped webs in grass. The wolf spider's robust build and alert, forward-facing eyes are distinctive once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: This species was originally classified in the genus Hogna until 2012, when scientists moved it to the genus Tigrosa based on genetic studies. There's also some historical naming confusion - a completely different spider species was accidentally given the same scientific name back in 1849, which sometimes causes mix-ups in older field guides.
compareHints: The Woodland Giant Wolf Spider is noticeably larger than its close relative, the Wetland Giant Wolf Spider, which prefers marshy areas rather than dry forests. While both are impressive in size, the Woodland Giant is the bulkier of the two and sticks to well-drained forest habitats. The Georgia Wolf Spider is primarily found further south and is less common in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Woodland Giant Wolf Spider (Tigrosa aspersa) is its closest New England relative but prefers drier habitats and has a more muted, brownish stripe rather than the bright yellow racing stripe.
The Georgia Wolf Spider is distinguished from its close relatives the Wetland Giant Wolf Spider and Woodland Giant Wolf Spider primarily by habitat preference and geographic origin.
